title: Processes and services
summary: A program on disk does nothing; a running copy of it is a process. Services are processes that run with no terminal, from boot.

text: A program is a file. Start it and the system makes a process: a running copy with its own memory and number, the PID.
- Run it twice, you get two processes. Stopping one leaves the other.
- Each process runs as a user, with that user's rights.

scheme: your terminal ───▶ ls, nano, a script
text: What you type runs in your terminal and usually ends with it.
- A service (or daemon) is a process with no terminal: it waits for work, often from boot to shutdown.
- On most Linux systems, systemd starts services, restarts one that crashes if its unit asks for it (Restart=), and keeps their logs. A Mac uses launchd.

scheme: ask:    please stop    saves, closes its files
2. force only if it won't stop
text: To stop a process, ask before forcing.
- Asked, a program can finish writing and clean up. Forced, it stops mid-way: broken files, leftover locks.
- A service is stopped through its manager (systemctl stop), so it stays stopped and the log says why.
- The Processes and Services lessons show the commands.
